note.text: A traditional school distinction separates formal logic, which examines the structure of reasoning, from material or applied assessment, which examines its content and truth. Other classifications distinguish deductive and inductive reasoning. These classifications answer different questions and should not be treated as identical. A valid deductive form preserves truth if its premises are true; checking that form does not establish the truth of the premises. Investigating a claim about a local market still requires evidence.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: A traditional school distinction separates formal logic, which examines the structure of reasoning, from material or applied assessment, which examines its content and truth. Other classifications distinguish deductive and inductive reasoning. These classifications answer different questions and should not be treated as identical. A valid deductive form preserves truth if its premises are true; checking that form does not establish the truth of the premises. Investigating a claim about a local market still requires evidence.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: Suppose all members of a hypothetical Buea club have cards and Ayuk is a member. The form supports the conclusion that Ayuk has a card. Whether that club really issued cards is a separate factual question. A survey predicting attendance from previous meetings makes another kind of move: it offers probable, not guaranteed, support.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Ask first whether the exercise concerns form, factual content or strength of inference. Do not label an argument false merely because its form is invalid: truth applies to statements, while validity applies to deductive reasoning. Traditional labels vary between textbooks; compare the reasoning task as well as the name.
